topic.subject: social
topic.title: How the State government works
topic.scope: MLAs, constituencies, majority, Chief Minister, Governor, legislature vs executive

misconceptions.statement: A constituency is the same as a district.
misconceptions.why: Students often conflate administrative boundaries with electoral boundaries.
misconceptions.fix: A constituency is an area specifically demarcated for electing a representative, which may not align with district borders.

probe.question: If a district has 5 lakh people, does it always have only one MLA?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because one district equals one constituency.

misconceptions.root_belief: Administrative units are identical to electoral units.

misconceptions.statement: Majority means getting the most votes among all candidates.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse 'majority' with 'plurality' (winning the most votes).
misconceptions.fix: Majority means having more than half the total number of seats in the assembly.

probe.question: If there are 100 seats, can a party with 30 seats form the government?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, if 30 is the highest number of seats any party got.

misconceptions.root_belief: Winning means having more than others.

misconceptions.statement: The Chief Minister is elected directly by the people of the state.
misconceptions.why: Students project the direct voting for an MLA onto the CM position.
misconceptions.fix: The CM is appointed by the Governor, usually being the leader of the party that won the majority of seats.

probe.question: Who votes directly for the Chief Minister?
probe.wrong_answer: The citizens of the state during the election.

misconceptions.root_belief: All leaders are chosen by direct public vote.

misconceptions.statement: The Governor makes all the laws for the state.
misconceptions.why: Students see the Governor as the 'boss' and assume they have absolute power.
misconceptions.fix: The Legislative Assembly makes the laws; the Governor gives formal assent to bills passed by the assembly.

probe.question: Who has the power to pass a new law in the state?
probe.wrong_answer: The Governor, because they are the head of the state.

misconceptions.root_belief: One powerful person makes all decisions.

misconceptions.statement: An MLA is a member of the state's government who works only for the party that is in power.
misconceptions.why: Students see MLAs of the ruling party in the news and assume the government is made up of one party's MLAs only.
misconceptions.fix: Every elected person in the Legislative Assembly is an MLA. MLAs of the ruling party and of the opposition all represent their constituency and all take part in the Assembly.

probe.question: An MLA belongs to the opposition party. Is that person still an MLA of the constituency?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only MLAs of the ruling party are real MLAs.

misconceptions.root_belief: Only ruling party members count as representatives

misconceptions.statement: An MLA is paid by the people of the constituency and must do whatever voters in the area ask.
misconceptions.why: Students think a representative is like a personal servant of the voters and has no duty to the whole state or to the law.
misconceptions.fix: An MLA represents the people of the constituency and raises their problems in the Assembly. The MLA also takes part in making laws for the whole state, and is paid by the state government.

probe.question: A voter asks the MLA to break a state rule for their family. What must the MLA do?
probe.wrong_answer: Do it, because the MLA must obey every voter.

misconceptions.root_belief: Representatives are servants who obey every voter

misconceptions.statement: The Legislative Assembly is the building where the Chief Minister and ministers work in their offices.
misconceptions.why: Students mix up the place with the people and the work done there, and confuse it with the Secretariat.
misconceptions.fix: The Legislative Assembly is the body of all the MLAs of the state. It meets to discuss problems, debate and make laws. The ministers' offices are separate.

probe.question: Who are the members of the Legislative Assembly?
probe.wrong_answer: The Chief Minister and the ministers only.

misconceptions.root_belief: Assembly means the government's office building

misconceptions.statement: Debate in the Assembly is just fighting and shouting, and it has no real use for the state.
misconceptions.why: Students see news clips of noisy walkouts and think debate is only arguing between parties.
misconceptions.fix: Debate lets MLAs of all parties question the government, discuss problems of the people and examine proposed laws before a decision is made.

probe.question: Why do MLAs debate a proposed law in the Assembly?
probe.wrong_answer: To fight with the other party and show who is stronger.

misconceptions.statement: The Governor chooses anyone he likes as Chief Minister, even a person who has no support of the MLAs.
misconceptions.why: Students know the Governor appoints the CM but miss the condition about majority support in the Assembly.
misconceptions.fix: The Governor appoints as Chief Minister the leader of the party or group that has the support of a majority of MLAs in the Assembly.

probe.question: Whom does the Governor appoint as Chief Minister?

misconceptions.root_belief: Appointing power means free personal choice

misconceptions.statement: The party that wins the most seats forms the government even if it is far short of half the MLAs.
misconceptions.why: Students link winning with being the largest party and forget that a government needs support of more than half the MLAs.
misconceptions.fix: A party or group needs the support of more than half the members of the Assembly to form the government. If no party has it, parties may join together.

probe.question: In an Assembly of 200 seats, a party wins 70 seats and others win less. Can it form the government alone?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it has won the most seats.

misconceptions.statement: The Governor is elected by the people of the state and belongs to the ruling party.
misconceptions.why: Students assume all important state posts are filled by voting like MLAs.
misconceptions.fix: The Governor is appointed by the central government (the President) and acts as the head of the state, not as an elected leader.

probe.question: How does a person become the Governor of a state?
probe.wrong_answer: By winning a vote of the people of the state.

misconceptions.root_belief: Every high office holder is elected by voters

misconceptions.statement: The Chief Minister has to leave office after five years even if the party still has a majority.
misconceptions.why: Students mix a fixed term with the MLAs' five-year term and think the CM is like a fixed-term post.
misconceptions.fix: The CM stays as long as he or she has the support of a majority of MLAs. After an election, a new Assembly is formed, and the leader with majority becomes CM, which can be the same person.

probe.question: A CM's party wins the next election with a majority. Can the same person be CM again?
probe.wrong_answer: No, one person cannot be CM for more than one term.

misconceptions.root_belief: Political posts have fixed one-term limits
